The Gorgeous Tasman Might Be the Family Tiny Home You’ve Been Dreaming Of
29 photos
Photo: Artisan Tiny Homes/Instagram
Even if you think you’ve seen all the dual-loft tiny homes out there, I promise you that The Tasman will surprise and delight you – this gorgeous home on wheels built in the equally-beautiful land of Tasmania, is meant to grow seamlessly from a couple’s elegant cocoon to a cozy haven for their young family.
Just as its name suggests, Artisan Tiny Homes is a brand where tiny living enthusiasts can find the impeccable craftsmanship, attention to detail, and exquisite customization that other mobile homes on the market lack. It’s safe to say that each of the approximately 35 tiny homes built here in almost a decade of activity is a work of art on wheels, sophisticated down to the smallest details and simply oozing personality.
The Tasman is no exception. Purpose-built for a young couple thinking about starting a family in the near future, this compact abode is meant to adapt to the growing needs of a family without major modifications. The solution sounds simple: a dual-loft layout, but the way it was actually envisioned and implemented is much more ingenious and with stunning results, compared to a basic, cookie-cutter version.
What you would typically see in a compact tiny house are two plain, open lofts placed at opposite ends of the layout, and accessed via separate staircases or ladders; these lofts are usually built with cheap materials, and have nothing more than a basic floor and a bed. It’s easy to see why many people shopping for a tiny house tend to avoid dual-loft designs, despite the advantage of having two extra rooms with the same compact footprint.
Photo: Artisan Tiny Homes This is where The Tasman takes a sharp turn to create two of the most beautiful, luxurious loft bedrooms you’ve ever seen. When stepping inside The Tasman, you are welcomed into a spacious open lounge, with high ceilings and no loft above it. A U-shaped kitchen occupies the middle section, alongside an elegant corridor that leads to the bathroom at the other end. The entire loft floor is built above this half of the layout, and accessed via a hidden staircase.
One of the major advantages of this unusual configuration is that both lofts are fully enclosed and, therefore, private. In many ways, they resemble conventional upstairs bedrooms, and this is one of them. The staircase is also unusual, and very practical in terms of space efficiency. It’s a split staircase, meaning that a shared base spreads into different staircases that lead to each bedroom, but it’s cleverly hidden next to the kitchen area.
Both the staircase and the two bedrooms are solidly built with high-quality materials, and it shows – even folks who fear the discomfort and potential safety risks of accessing loft bedrooms will feel perfectly comfortable using this split staircase and accessing both of these rooms on a daily basis. VJ lining boards throughout, waterproof laminate flooring, and large windows further elevate the quality of these lofts.
The main bedroom features a super-comfy walk-around bed, flanked by large windows. The best part? It even features a full-size, floor-to-ceiling wardrobe with more than enough room for the personal items of two people, which is something you rarely find in a tiny house bedroom. The wall with custom-built shutters is visible from the downstairs lounge, and you can see that the bedroom itself is fully private.
Photo: Artisan Tiny Homes The second bedroom is seen more as a multi-purpose space that can evolve as the family grows. Until the first baby is born, the owners can use it a guest room or a hobby/office room. Then, it can be turned seamlessly into an adorable nursery, and then again into a child’s bedroom. The floor space is generous enough for a beautiful baby cradle, and a single bed later on, while large windows (one on each side) fill it with natural light.
The Tasman’s kitchen is also envisioned as a family space. The U-shaped design incorporates generous cupboard space, including a full-height pantry and a dedicated fridge tower. High-quality, full-size appliances are also seamlessly incorporated, and there’s still a generous counter surface left for preparing meals. The outer edge at one end is oversized, in order to double as a breakfast for the whole family – informal and space-efficient.
Even the bathroom is a beautiful space with its own personality. It’s big enough to house a full-size, modern shower cabin, a vintage-style vanity, and a toilet (which is a composting version, for that added touch of sustainability). The blue-and-white checkerboard tiles truly bring this bathroom to life, and the inset shelves inside the shower cabin are another modern touch.
Last, but certainly not least, The Tasman’s lounge is an inviting, warm oasis for the whole family (plus guests). Furniture is kept to a minimum, with just a custom-crafted, elegant sofa that hides storage underneath, and an adorable wood-burning stove that makes the ambiance even cozier. The uninterrupted, generous ceiling height is what makes this lounge feel superbly comfortable, with natural light coming through the glazed main entrance and two windows.
Photo: Artisan Tiny Homes Style-wise, The Tasman exudes the timeless elegance of a modern classic. White VJ walls throughout create that familiar farmhouse aesthetic, beautifully complemented by the darker flooring and natural timber countertops in the kitchen. The buttery shade of the cabinetry in both the kitchen and the bathroom adds a subtle vintage touch, matching the hardware and the large, farmhouse-style sinks.
Lighting also combined modern LED options with romantic hanging light fixtures and chandeliers. Large windows in every room keep this entire tiny house bathed in natural light, which makes its smart layout feel even more spacious.
Judging by this gorgeous interior, you would think that The Tasman must be an XL home on wheels, but its compact footprint doesn’t exceed 8 meters in length (27.8 feet), 2.4 meters (7.8 feet) in width, and 4.3 meters (14 feet) in height. In the words of its own builder, what matters most is not a big house, but one that is cleverly designed.
The gorgeous Tasman starts out as a fully functional, elegant tiny house for a couple, and is ready to morph into a family tiny home over time, once their first baby is born. The Tasman’s dual-loft layout offers much more than the flexibility of a spare bedroom; it creates the privacy, luminosity, storage, and comfort that differentiate real bedrooms from basic loft spaces. This is the kind of tiny home that can truly be loved and enjoyed for generations.
Photo: Artisan Tiny Homes With tiny homes like this beautiful Tasmanian custom-build, downsizing can become a first option, not a second thought. Wonderful craftsmanship, high-quality materials, and a well-planned layout can make the difference between a simple house on wheels and a true home. And let’s not forget beauty – a forever tiny home must look and feel beautiful, and this is where Artisan Tiny Homes truly excels.
Kerrie, and artist and interior designer, is the one who brings these lovely tiny homes to life as if she had a magic wand, together with her husband Kevin, a builder and a restorer, and their daughter who is also a carpenter. Who better than this talented family to know what a family needs in a tiny house? The Tasman is just one of their many custom creations that make dreams come true.

In 1968, Plymouth had three B-body cars in showrooms. In addition to the bread-and-butter Belvedere, it also offered the premium Satellite and the GTX. The latter was an upscale muscle car. That year, it introduced the Road Runner as its fourth intermediate.
The latter filled another gap between the Belvedere and the GTX. It was similar to the latter, as in it was restricted to two-door body styles and big-block V8 engines. However, it lacked the GTX's premium features and came standard with the 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) V8. The GTX featured the larger 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB in base form.
The lack of fancy features and the standard 383 V8 made the Road Runner notably more affordable than the GTX. As a result, it was also far more popular. Plymouth sold over 44,000 examples in 1968 alone, more than the total GTX production between 1967 and 1971. In 1969, Road Runner sales reached an all-time high with over 81,000 examples delivered.
This number makes the 1969 Road Runner one of the most common muscle cars from the golden era. However, that changes when the standard 383-cubic-inch V8 is replaced with any of the optional powertrains. In 1969, the list included both the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Six-Barrel and the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi.
The former was brand-new for 1969 and included in the A12 package. The bundle had several heavy-duty items that turned the Road Runner into a drag-ready vehicle. Only 1,412 units were ordered with the A12 package.
The Hemi was carried over from 1968 and found its way into far fewer examples. Records show that 787 examples were fitted with the 425-horsepower V8. The number is split between 421 hardtops, 356 coupes, and 10 convertibles. A little more than half of these cars got the four-speed manual , with the others equipped with the three-speed TorqueFlite automatic.
The stunning Mopar you see here is one of those rigs ordered with the desirable four-speed manual gearbox. It's one of 234 hardtops fitted with the Hemi/manual setup and a one-of-one gem due to its color and trim combo. This Road Runner is a very formal car finished in black and with white upholstery. It also has a bench front seat.
The hardtop appears to be in amazing condition, which isn't surprising given that it was restored on a rotisserie in 2013. Moreover, it was stripped down to bare metal and repainted earlier in 2026. It has a numbers-matching drivetrain, and it's a Super Track Pak model with a Dana 60 rear end with 4.10 gears.
The Mopar was recently added to the lots of Mecum's Kissimmee 2027 auction , which takes place in January. It's one of 17 Hemi-powered classics scheduled to cross the block at the event, and it will change hands for a six-figure sum. I'm pretty sure it will sell for over $200,000.

By: Staff Writer November 27, 2026
The Çöpler gold mine in eastern Turkey has resumed processing stockpiled ore more than two years after a heap leach failure killed nine workers, Bloomberg reported Wednesday.
Operator Anagold Madencilik began treating the ore at its pressure oxidation plant in the third quarter under a temporary operating licence, a company spokesperson told the news agency.
Anagold aims to produce about 1.3 tonnes of gold by year-end, equivalent to roughly 41,800 ounces. The mine produced 6.9 tonnes in 2023, or about a fifth of Turkey’s total output that year.
The restart comes as Turkey seeks to expand domestic gold production and reduce its dependence on imports. Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar told a parliamentary committee Nov. 23 that the government’s goal is annual production of 100 tonnes. He gave no deadline for the target.
The resumption follows the exit of SSR Mining (TSX, Nasdaq: SSRM), which is based in the United States. The company completed the sale of its 80% stake in Çöpler and related properties to Turkish conglomerate Cengiz Holding and affiliates on June 24 for about $1.5 billion (C$2.1 billion) in cash after adjustments. Turkey’s Lidya Madencilik holds the remaining 20%.
Environmental fallout
The February 2024 heap leach failure sent material into the nearby Sabırlı Valley and Manganese Pit, burying nine workers. All nine bodies had been recovered by June that year, according to SSR.
Turkish authorities revoked the mine’s environmental permit after the disaster. SSR spent $149.3 million on reclamation and remediation at the site through the end of 2025.
The landslide also raised concerns about potential cyanide contamination of the Euphrates River. Turkey’s deputy environment minister told parliament in May 2024 that surface and groundwater analyses had found no adverse effects from cyanide.
The disaster marked the second major operational disruption at Çöpler in less than two years. In June 2022, Turkey’s environment ministry ordered a production halt after a pipeline leaked diluted cyanide solution.
Legal proceedings over the fatal landslide continue. A trial involving 43 defendants accused of causing deaths and injuries through negligence last convened Oct. 20. The court scheduled the next hearing for Jan. 26, 2027, while awaiting a new expert report, Turkish news outlet Bianet reported. Print

By Gavin van Marle
27 November 2026
Container spot freight rates on the Asia-Mediterranean trade were the only deepsea route prices that gained this week, as Transpacific and Asia-Europe rates further diverged.
According to this week’s World Container Index (WCI) by Drewry, its spot rate for Shanghai-Genoa saw an 8% week-on-week increase, to end at $4,802 per 40ft, while Shanghai-Rotterdam was unchanged for a second week. at $3,485 per 40ft.
Meanwhile, next week could see a renewed hike in Asia-Europe spot rates, with carriers clearly shaping up to push for higher short-term prices for December with a series of peak season surcharges (PSS) scheduled to be applied on 1 December.
Justified on the basis of an early Chinese New Year in 2027, both CMA CGM and Hapag-Lloyd have set a PSS of $1,000 per 40ft on Asia-North Europe shipments. Hapag-Lloyd also introducing a $1,500 per 40ft PSS on Asia-Mediterranean bookings on the same day.
These are expected to be supported by further surcharges and new FAK levels introduced by other carriers next month. Maersk has set a PSS of $1,500 per 40ft for Asia-North Europe and $2,000 per 40ft to the Mediterranean, both for implementation on 14 December.
On the same day, MSC will revise its FAK pricing on the two routes – rising from $4,600 to $5,600 per 40ft on Asia-North Europe, and a much more aggressive $7,500 per 40ft on Asia-Mediterranean shipments, currently $5,300 per 40ft, following its 15 November FAK notice.
Xeneta chief analyst Peter Sand said the price hikes were beginning to filter into the platform’s short-term rate outlook.
“Early Xeneta data indicates average spot rates to Mediterranean will increase a further 10% to 15% at the start of December, having already increased 27% since 14 October.
“An uptick is also expected into North Europe,” he added.
While next week’s rate increases are set to be accompanied by a higher degree of blanked sailings – Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight records seven – three Asia-North Europe and four Asia-Mediterranean – for next week, compared with four that took place this week, three Asia-North Europe and one Asia- Mediterranean.
The forecast December rate increases will coincide with predictions that capacity next month could be among the highest on record.
“Rates for the last week of November range from $2,700 to $3,200 per 40ft, against last week’s SCFI [Shanghai International Freight Index] assessment at $3,356 per 40ft, with capacity pressure building and December sailings expected to reach a new record high,” Linerlytica noted this week.
The analyst’s forward-looking capacity projections are for a monthly average of 400,000 teu capacity a week in December, up from around 350,000 teu a week this month.
According to Xeneta data, current capacity into North Europe is 4.9% higher than a month ago, and up 6.7% to the Mediterranean.
With yesterday’s Thanksgiving holiday bringing a quiet week on the Transpacific trade, rates on the WCI’s Shanghai-Los Angeles route fell 8% week on week, to end at $6,437 per 40ft, while its Shanghai-New York leg was down 7%, to $7,615 per 40ft.
“The upward trend into Europe contrasts with fronthauls into the US, where early Xeneta data indicates further spot rate declines at the start of December,” Mr Sand said. “Average spot rates have already fallen 12% into US east coast and 7.6% into US west coast since 14 October.
“The most recent Xeneta data paints a rosier picture for US shippers, but a wider market perspective changes the situation dramatically: despite the softening in October and November, average spot rates to US west coast remain up 310%, compared with pre-Hormuz crisis levels on 28 February. Into the US east coast, average spot rates are up 283%.
“From the Far East to Mediterranean and North Europe, the recent increases mean average spot rates are up a much smaller 54% and 53% respectively, compared with pre-Hormuz crisis levels,” he added.

The vehicle features 20-inch front and 21-inch rear wheels, a power-operated sunroof, leather and Sport-Tex upholstery, heated front seats with power adjustment, a Bose premium sound system, a surround view camera system, and an extended-range fuel tank. It is presented in Vanadium Gray Metallic, and other than the dashcam, it has zero modifications.
Power is supplied by a flat-six (d’oh) engine with twin-turbocharging, and a 3.0-liter displacement. It produces 388 hp (343 ps/252 kW ) and 332 lb-ft (450 Nm) of torque, with everything channeled to the rear wheels through a six-speed manual transmission. The 0-60 mph (0-97 kph) takes a little over 4 seconds, and on summer tires, the Porsche 911 Carrera T Coupe hits up to 183 mph (295 kph).
This 992 is accompanied by the owner’s manuals, the window sticker, some service records, and two keys. It’s worth noting that there is a loan on this car, and the sale proceeds will be used to satisfy it, as only then the title will become available. Interested parties should also know that full PPF has been applied to the vehicle’s exterior. The windshield sits under a clear protection film, and the windows have been ceramic tinted.
The Porsche 911 in question is advertised on Cars&Bids, with a high bid of $100,911 at the time of writing, and six days left in the ongoing online auction. The gavel will hit the table on December 3, 2026, and if you want it, then you can bid on it here .
